Adult ADHD

By: Mosibudi Ratlebjane | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We explore the Personal and Professional costs of Adults living with ADHD, in an already distracted Digital age?

Unique Selling Point:
In a slight moment of disorganisation, the phrase often used in social settings is "I might clearly have ADHD." Widely known as a neurological disorder effecting mainly children, Adult ADHD patients, largely go undiagnosed for the better part of their lives. The misconceptions, around Adult ADHD, run far with the stigma of being lazy, disorganised, and unable to complete tasks lay bare the harsher ramifications for adults as the stakes become higher while navigate adult life.

Adult Women have been reportedly found to be diagnosed later in life, And in a recent article, found that the Lockdown Pandemic exacerbated symptoms of ADHD in women leading to prevalent diagnosis, due to the breakdown of routine and overwhelming pressures of taking care of the household and work all in the same place. This is something most people without this diagnosis, have gone through. But in a quest to dispel some of the misconceptions about ADHD, this story will investigate the Why ADHD is real and not just a symptom of momentarily lapse of judgement, or inattentiveness.

Summary:
Described by some, as a life of perpetual failure, Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) has received increased scientific, clinical and public attention over the past few decades and is now recognised as a common neurodevelopment disorder, present throughout life, with a chronic, costly and debilitating course if untreated. Unfortunately, many patients suffering from ADHD remain undiagnosed, or if diagnosed, they do not receive optimal treatment.

Improved outcomes are possible if patients suffering from ADHD receive a timely and accurate diagnosis, and receive comprehensive care, which would include psychopharmacological interventions, behavioural interventions and support. Previous research established the knowledge gap amongst general practitioners with regard to adult ADHD.




Further information:
In South Africa (SA), poor identification and treatment of common mental disorders at primary healthcare level, limited access to specialist resources and a large service delivery and treatment gap remain problematic. In the current environment of a pressured health care system, GPs will play an increasingly important role in the early identification and management of adults with ADHD.

Extrapolating from population statistics (based on StatsSA population statistics for SA) and known prevalence information, we calculated the expected number of adults in SA between the ages of 20 and 50 affected by ADHD to be around 1 million.

Although they may appear to function well, excessive amounts of energy and time are used to accomplish tasks.

Script:


VOICE:


VOICE: We all remember having that one classmate, who struggled to “sit still, follow instructions, or always had something to say at the wrong time.
LINK: It’s in the classroom like this that most learners will start presenting with symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity, but for many children in South Africa especially young girls who fall through the cracks of diagnosis, only to be diagnosed later in their adult life.


Clip_001 _ (9:11) _CONFIDENCE TSOLO:
I've always known that I had something, but I just didn't know it was called ADHD. I mean, I'm really super hyper from being a kid. As a child, people would be like, No, no, no, stop it. Stop it. They don’t really know that you don’t have control.


VOICE: It's been a mere four months since Confidence Tsolo was diagnosed with ADHD, at age 36. She recalls her hidden academic horrors as a young girl, with a nagging feeling that something was different about her.


Clip_001_(3:21) _CONFIDENCE TSOLO: Sho, say my school is very difficult.
I || (3:33) I like to have to work three times harder than a person without ADHD. Clip_001_(3:59)_CONFIDENCE TSOLO: I would lose interest while studying. Imagine studying for a test then now all of a sudden you lose interest.

Clip_001_(4:29) CONFIDENCE TSOLO: I don't like reading a book from one to page 469 for an example, I like to see visuals.
A sales marketer in the finance industry. The mother of two, had developed a routined and active schedule around her life. Until lockdown hit- forcing her to work from home - alone- bringing back all the anxiety she felt, as a little girl.


(12:54) CONFIDENCE TSOLO_ All my coping mechanisms were taken away from me. My coping mechanisms being Netball, being running, you know, now I have to be confined in a small space and work from home. My anxiety is very, very high. forgetting where I'm putting my keys and, and, and the kind of job that I do. It's super technical. So I need to always be on the ball.


VOICE: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, is a neurodevelopmental disorder that is
closely related to the executive function of our brains. That's our cognitive ability that enables us to plan, focus, remember instructions, and self-regulate our behaviour.


(06:56) _T001_DR R Schoeman: ADHD is another invisible disorder with manifestations in real life. But often the patient with ADHD, there's a lot of embarrassment, there's a very poor self-esteem, about my ability to cope with things that other people seem to take in their stride.


VOICE: Psychiatrist Professor Renata Schoeman, says poor identification and treatment in Adults with ADHD is of great concern, as the direct and indirect cause and effect of the condition can be dire for undiagnosed Adults.

T001_(2:40) DR R. Schoeman: So someone with ADHD there's a biological reason and a deficit in the brain that causes them to struggle with inattentiveness, hyperactivity, impulsivity, and also emotional regulation that can very present in various ways in children, we can see emotional difficulties, behavioural difficulties or poor academic performance.

T001(3:06)_DR R Schoeman: But as adults might also be faced with comorbid medical conditions, whether it's poorly controlled health issues, but specifically also mental health disorders, substance abuse, depression, anxiety. And what the people around them might see is disorganisation, poor time management, and tardiness.

Voice: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual For Mental Disorders describes ADHD as a persistent pattern of behaviour . Where symptoms of inattentiveness, hyperactivity and impulsivity must persist for six months or more.

VOICE: A 2017 South African study, estimated that at least 1 million adults between the ages of 20 to 50 were affected by ADHD. Many of whom face years of misdiagnosis, with a treatment gap of up to 75% .

LINK: LIKE MOST MENTAL ILLNESSES HAVING ADHD IT ISN'T MUCH OF A CHOICE, YOU COULD BE A DOCTOR, SOFTWARE DEVELOPER OR EVEN A PSYCHOLOGIST. AND FOR MOST PEOPLE LIVING WITH ADHD, LEADING A PRODUCTIVE CAREER COMES WITH GREAT ANXIETY.


T0043 (0:47)_ Michelle Munro, Have you ever heard the circus March the dead a little at that. It's kind of like that. You've got a million thoughts running through your head at one moment, you cannot decide which one to follow through with. It causes a large amount of anxiety, irritability, probably to the point of aggressiveness because your brain just cannot allow you to just take a moment to breathe, you know, take the edge off.


VOICE: Masking over symptoms is something professional nurse Michelle Munro knows all too well. Diagnosed at age eleven, while living overseas. She stopped treating her ADHD for two decades, when it all came to a halt early this year.

T043_(6:40) Michelle Munro: Lack of concentration, impulse control, fidgeting, the knots sitting still, that's just the tip of the iceberg. You're not seeing what's happening underneath, which is the debilitating self-confidence issues.
Michelle Munor _Everything was just continuously overwhelming, just stressful to the point where I felt like I couldn't function in daily life.

Voice: Michelle, has felt a stark difference since going back on her medication, something Dr Schoeman says employers can also help in creating conducive work environments, to help with productivity.
T001_ (21:23) Dr R Schoeman: I think it's important that employers become more well versed with how ADHD can present and maybe that person that you appointed, or you recruited, because you saw the brilliance in them, and now they're in your employment and they're not performing.
T0043_(3:25)Michelle Munor_Comparing myself to five years ago, and now in a work setup. This is the first time in my life that I have kept a job for the amount of time that I have. And that for me is huge.
(00:00: Francois Greybe)
When people hear ADHD, they automatically assume it's the kid bouncing around. (0:49) Exactly. So, my brain is bouncing off the walls inside my head, Whereas My body is quite happy to sit still.

VOICE: It has been 12 years since forty-five-year-old Francois Greybe- A software developer, and his wife Debie found out about Francois’ ADHD diagnosis.
MAC-Farlance: (17:24) So what would you say are some of the challenges, with someone who has had, you know, having children being a family man, what was that like?

(17:31) Francois Greybe_I wasn't able to perform, like my peers and my colleagues at work. Especially once things started to when I became more senior, and so on and so forth. You know, then I started experiencing a hell of a lot of stress. And that would obviously come home with it.
(4:16) Debbie: We, I will not say that we don't fight and have many arguments and many disagreements. But I do feel that compared to then we are in a far better stable state.


VOICE: Francois relies on medication everyday, which can be a costly exercise, as some Medical Aids in South Africa do not cover medication for patients or members over the age of 18.

Francois Greybe:
The medical aids or at least my medical aid doesn't doesn't cover ADHD medication on chronic. So that is an out of pocket expense every month. I think in the region, I stand corrected, but for about 1500 Rand a month for my medication.

VIOICE: The Council for Medical Schemes confirmed that although it recognises ADHD as a psychiatric disorder, it’s not listed yet as a prescribed minimum benefit, which leaves the decision to fund treatment and medicines up to medical schemes individually.
For Michelle, Francois and Confidence, they have no regrets of the past and live everyday kinder to their inner child.

(32:06)_Confidence Tsolo_I would say to my younger self about having this condition, you are normal, there's nothing wrong with you. You are just perfect just the way you are. And you can be anything you want to be. You know, as long as there's mechanisms in place to help you get there.
